# trybuild - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/trybuild/1.0.117/target-redirect/trybuild/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#a-compiler-diagnostics-testing-library-in-just-3-functions) A compiler diagnostics testing library in just 3 functions.

Trybuild is a test harness for invoking rustc on a set of test cases and asserting that any resulting error messages are the ones intended.

Such tests are commonly useful for testing error reporting involving procedural macros. We would write test cases triggering either errors detected by the macro or errors detected by the Rust compiler in the resulting expanded code, and compare against the expected errors to ensure that they remain user-friendly.

This style of testing is sometimes called *ui tests* because they test
aspects of the user’s interaction with a library outside of what would be
covered by ordinary API tests.

Nothing here is specific to macros; trybuild would work equally well for testing misuse of non-macro APIs.

[§](https://docs.rs#compile-fail-tests)Compile-fail tests

A minimal trybuild setup looks like this:

```
#[test]
fn ui() {
    let t = trybuild::TestCases::new();
    t.compile_fail("tests/ui/*.rs");
}
```
The test can be run with `cargo test`. It will individually compile each of
the source files matching the glob pattern, expect them to fail to compile,
and assert that the compiler’s error message matches an adjacently named
**.stderr* file containing the expected output (same file name as the test
except with a different extension). If it matches, the test case is
considered to succeed.

Dependencies listed under `[dev-dependencies]` in the project’s Cargo.toml
are accessible from within the test cases.

Failing tests display the expected vs actual compiler output inline.

A compile_fail test that fails to fail to compile is also a failure.

[§](https://docs.rs#pass-tests)Pass tests

The same test harness is able to run tests that are expected to pass, too.
Ordinarily you would just have Cargo run such tests directly, but being able
to combine modes like this could be useful for workshops in which
participants work through test cases enabling one at a time. Trybuild was
originally developed for my [procedural macros workshop at Rust
Latam](https://github.com/dtolnay/proc-macro-workshop).

```
#[test]
fn ui() {
    let t = trybuild::TestCases::new();
    t.pass("tests/01-parse-header.rs");
    t.pass("tests/02-parse-body.rs");
    t.compile_fail("tests/03-expand-four-errors.rs");
    t.pass("tests/04-paste-ident.rs");
    t.pass("tests/05-repeat-section.rs");
    //t.pass("tests/06-make-work-in-function.rs");
    //t.pass("tests/07-init-array.rs");
    //t.compile_fail("tests/08-ident-span.rs");
}
```
Pass tests are considered to succeed if they compile successfully and have a
`main` function that does not panic when the compiled binary is executed.

[§](https://docs.rs#details)Details

That’s the entire API.

[§](https://docs.rs#workflow)Workflow

There are two ways to update the **.stderr* files as you iterate on your
test cases or your library; handwriting them is not recommended.

First, if a test case is being run as compile_fail but a corresponding
**.stderr* file does not exist, the test runner will save the actual
compiler output with the right filename into a directory called *wip* within
the directory containing Cargo.toml. So you can update these files by
deleting them, running `cargo test`, and moving all the files from *wip*
into your testcase directory.

Alternatively, run `cargo test` with the environment variable
`TRYBUILD=overwrite` to skip the *wip* directory and write all compiler
output directly in place. You’ll want to check `git diff` afterward to be
sure the compiler’s output is what you had in mind.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-to-test)What to test

When it comes to compile-fail tests, write tests for anything for which you care to find out when there are changes in the user-facing compiler output. As a negative example, please don’t write compile-fail tests simply calling all of your public APIs with arguments of the wrong type; there would be no benefit.

A common use would be for testing specific targeted error messages emitted
by a procedural macro. For example the derive macro from the [ ref-cast](https://github.com/dtolnay/ref-cast)
crate is required to be placed on a type that has either

`#[repr(C)]` or
`#[repr(transparent)]` in order for the expansion to be free of undefined
behavior, which it enforces at compile time:```
error: RefCast trait requires #[repr(C)] or #[repr(transparent)]
 --> $DIR/missing-repr.rs:3:10
  |
3 | #[derive(RefCast)]
  |          ^^^^^^^
```
Macros that consume helper attributes will want to check that unrecognized content within those attributes is properly indicated to the caller. Is the error message correctly placed under the erroneous tokens, not on a useless call_site span?

```
error: unknown serde field attribute `qqq`
 --> $DIR/unknown-attribute.rs:5:13
  |
5 |     #[serde(qqq = "...")]
  |             ^^^
```
Declarative macros can benefit from compile-fail tests too. The [ json!](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1.0/serde_json/macro.json.html)
macro from serde_json is just a great big macro_rules macro but makes an
effort to have error messages from broken JSON in the input always appear on
the most appropriate token:

```
error: no rules expected the token `,`
 --> $DIR/double-comma.rs:4:38
  |
4 |     println!("{}", json!({ "k": null,, }));
  |                                      ^ no rules expected this token in macro call
```
Sometimes we may have a macro that expands successfully but we count on it
to trigger particular compiler errors at some point beyond macro expansion.
For example the [ readonly](https://github.com/dtolnay/readonly) crate introduces struct fields that are public
but readable only, even if the caller has a &mut reference to the
surrounding struct. If someone writes to a readonly field, we need to be
sure that it wouldn’t compile:

```
error[E0594]: cannot assign to data in a `&` reference
  --> $DIR/write-a-readonly.rs:17:26
   |
17 |     println!("{}", s.n); s.n += 1;
   |                          ^^^^^^^^ cannot assign
```
In all of these cases, the compiler’s output can change because our crate or one of our dependencies broke something, or as a consequence of changes in the Rust compiler. Both are good reasons to have well conceived compile-fail tests. If we refactor and mistakenly cause an error that used to be correct to now no longer be emitted or be emitted in the wrong place, that is important for a test suite to catch. If the compiler changes something that makes error messages that we care about substantially worse, it is also important to catch and report as a compiler issue.

[§](https://docs.rs#troubleshooting)Troubleshooting

The Rust compiler’s diagnostic output can vary as a function of whether the
`rust-src` Rustup component is installed. The compiler will render source
snippets from the standard library if the standard library source is
available locally, and will simply omit snippets if not. This can account
for differences between CI and local development.

If you have compile_fail tests pertaining to standard library traits or types, you can ensure a consistent environment by adding a rust-toolchain.toml file with the following content.

```
[toolchain]
components = ["rust-src"]
```

That’s the entire API.

[§](https://docs.rs#workflow)Workflow

There are two ways to update the **.stderr* files as you iterate on your
test cases or your library; handwriting them is not recommended.

First, if a test case is being run as compile_fail but a corresponding
**.stderr* file does not exist, the test runner will save the actual
compiler output with the right filename into a directory called *wip* within
the directory containing Cargo.toml. So you can update these files by
deleting them, running `cargo test`, and moving all the files from *wip*
into your testcase directory.

Alternatively, run `cargo test` with the environment variable
`TRYBUILD=overwrite` to skip the *wip* directory and write all compiler
output directly in place. You’ll want to check `git diff` afterward to be
sure the compiler’s output is what you had in mind.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-to-test)What to test

When it comes to compile-fail tests, write tests for anything for which you care to find out when there are changes in the user-facing compiler output. As a negative example, please don’t write compile-fail tests simply calling all of your public APIs with arguments of the wrong type; there would be no benefit.

A common use would be for testing specific targeted error messages emitted
by a procedural macro. For example the derive macro from the [ ref-cast](https://github.com/dtolnay/ref-cast)
crate is required to be placed on a type that has either

`#[repr(C)]` or
`#[repr(transparent)]` in order for the expansion to be free of undefined
behavior, which it enforces at compile time:```
error: RefCast trait requires #[repr(C)] or #[repr(transparent)]
 --> $DIR/missing-repr.rs:3:10
  |
3 | #[derive(RefCast)]
  |          ^^^^^^^
```
Macros that consume helper attributes will want to check that unrecognized content within those attributes is properly indicated to the caller. Is the error message correctly placed under the erroneous tokens, not on a useless call_site span?

```
error: unknown serde field attribute `qqq`
 --> $DIR/unknown-attribute.rs:5:13
  |
5 |     #[serde(qqq = "...")]
  |             ^^^
```
Declarative macros can benefit from compile-fail tests too. The [ json!](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1.0/serde_json/macro.json.html)
macro from serde_json is just a great big macro_rules macro but makes an
effort to have error messages from broken JSON in the input always appear on
the most appropriate token:

```
error: no rules expected the token `,`
 --> $DIR/double-comma.rs:4:38
  |
4 |     println!("{}", json!({ "k": null,, }));
  |                                      ^ no rules expected this token in macro call
```
Sometimes we may have a macro that expands successfully but we count on it
to trigger particular compiler errors at some point beyond macro expansion.
For example the [ readonly](https://github.com/dtolnay/readonly) crate introduces struct fields that are public
but readable only, even if the caller has a &mut reference to the
surrounding struct. If someone writes to a readonly field, we need to be
sure that it wouldn’t compile:

```
error[E0594]: cannot assign to data in a `&` reference
  --> $DIR/write-a-readonly.rs:17:26
   |
17 |     println!("{}", s.n); s.n += 1;
   |                          ^^^^^^^^ cannot assign
```
In all of these cases, the compiler’s output can change because our crate or one of our dependencies broke something, or as a consequence of changes in the Rust compiler. Both are good reasons to have well conceived compile-fail tests. If we refactor and mistakenly cause an error that used to be correct to now no longer be emitted or be emitted in the wrong place, that is important for a test suite to catch. If the compiler changes something that makes error messages that we care about substantially worse, it is also important to catch and report as a compiler issue.

[§](https://docs.rs#troubleshooting)Troubleshooting

The Rust compiler’s diagnostic output can vary as a function of whether the
`rust-src` Rustup component is installed. The compiler will render source
snippets from the standard library if the standard library source is
available locally, and will simply omit snippets if not. This can account
for differences between CI and local development.

If you have compile_fail tests pertaining to standard library traits or types, you can ensure a consistent environment by adding a rust-toolchain.toml file with the following content.

```
[toolchain]
components = ["rust-src"]
```

# json in serde_json - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_json/1.0/serde_json/macro.json.html

```
macro_rules! json {
    ($($json:tt)+) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Construct a `serde_json::Value` from a JSON literal.

```
let value = json!({
    "code": 200,
    "success": true,
    "payload": {
        "features": [
            "serde",
            "json"
        ],
        "homepage": null
    }
});
```
Variables or expressions can be interpolated into the JSON literal. Any type
interpolated into an array element or object value must implement Serde’s
`Serialize` trait, while any type interpolated into an object key must
implement `Into<String>`. If the `Serialize` implementation of the
interpolated type decides to fail, or if the interpolated type contains a
map with non-string keys, the `json!` macro will panic.

```
let code = 200;
let features = vec!["serde", "json"];
let value = json!({
    "code": code,
    "success": code == 200,
    "payload": {
        features[0]: features[1]
    }
});
```
Trailing commas are allowed inside both arrays and objects.

```
let value = json!([
    "notice",
    "the",
    "trailing",
    "comma -->",
]);
```

# derive_builder - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/derive_builder/0.20.2/target-redirect/derive_builder/index.html

## Expand description

Derive a builder for a struct

This crate implements the [builder pattern](https://web.archive.org/web/20170701044756/https://aturon.github.io/ownership/builders.html) for you.
Just apply `#[derive(Builder)]` to a struct `Foo`, and it will derive an additional
struct `FooBuilder` with **setter**-methods for all fields and a **build**-method
— the way you want it.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

Add `derive_builder` as a dependency to you `Cargo.toml`.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-you-write)What you write

```
use derive_builder::Builder;
#[derive(Builder)]
struct Lorem {
    ipsum: u32,
    // ..
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#what-you-get)What you get

```
#[derive(Clone, Default)]
struct LoremBuilder {
    ipsum: Option<u32>,
}
#[allow(dead_code)]
impl LoremBuilder {
    pub fn ipsum(&mut self, value: u32) -> &mut Self {
        let mut new = self;
        new.ipsum = Some(value);
        new
    }
    fn build(&self) -> Result<Lorem, LoremBuilderError> {
        Ok(Lorem {
            ipsum: Clone::clone(self.ipsum
                .as_ref()
                .ok_or(LoremBuilderError::from(UninitializedFieldError::new("ipsum")))?),
        })
    }
}
```
By default all generated setter-methods take and return `&mut self`
(aka *non-consuming* builder pattern). Accordingly, the build method also takes a
reference by default.

You can easily opt into different patterns and control many other aspects.

The build method returns `Result<T, E>`, where `T` is the struct you started with
and E is a generated builder error type.
It returns `Err` if you didn’t initialize all fields and no default values were
provided.

[§](https://docs.rs#builder-patterns)Builder Patterns

Let’s look again at the example above. You can now build structs like this:

`let x: Lorem = LoremBuilder::default().ipsum(42).build()?;`Ok, *chaining* method calls is nice, but what if `ipsum(42)` should only happen if `geek = true`?

So let’s make this call conditional

```
let mut builder = LoremBuilder::default();
if geek {
    builder.ipsum(42);
}
let x: Lorem = builder.build()?;
```
Now it comes in handy that our setter methods take and return mutable references. Otherwise
we would need to write something more clumsy like `builder = builder.ipsum(42)` to reassign
the return value each time we have to call a setter conditionally.

Setters with mutable references are therefore a convenient default for the builder pattern in Rust.

But this is a free world and the choice is still yours!

[§](https://docs.rs#owned-aka-consuming)Owned, aka Consuming

Precede your struct (or field) with `#[builder(pattern = "owned")]` to opt into this pattern.
Builders generated with this pattern do not automatically derive `Clone`, which allows builders
to be generated for structs with fields that do not derive `Clone`.

- Setters take and return `self`.
- PRO: Setter calls and final build method can be chained.
- CON: If you don’t chain your calls, you have to create a reference to each return value,
e.g. `builder = builder.ipsum(42)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#mutable-aka-non-consuming-recommended)Mutable, aka Non-Consuming (recommended)

This pattern is recommended and active by default if you don’t specify anything else.
You can precede your struct (or field) with `#[builder(pattern = "mutable")]`
to make this choice explicit.

- Setters take and return `&mut self`.
- PRO: Setter calls and final build method can be chained.
- CON: The build method must clone or copy data to create something owned out of a
mutable reference. Otherwise it could not be used in a chain. **(*)**

[§](https://docs.rs#immutable)Immutable

Precede your struct (or field) with `#[builder(pattern = "immutable")]` to opt into this pattern.

- Setters take and return `&self`.
- PRO: Setter calls and final build method can be chained.
- CON: If you don’t chain your calls, you have to create a reference to each return value,
e.g. `builder = builder.ipsum(42)`.
- CON: The build method *and each setter*must clone or copy data to create something owned out of a reference.**(*)**

[§](https://docs.rs#-performance-considerations)(*) Performance Considerations

Luckily Rust is clever enough to optimize these clone-calls away in release builds
for your every-day use cases. Thats quite a safe bet - we checked this for you. ;-)
Switching to consuming signatures (=`self`) is unlikely to give you any performance
gain, but very likely to restrict your API for non-chained use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#more-features)More Features

[§](https://docs.rs#hidden-fields)Hidden Fields

You can hide fields by skipping their setters on (and presence in) the builder struct.

- Opt-out — skip setters via `#[builder(setter(skip))]`on individual fields.
- Opt-in — set `#[builder(setter(skip))]`on the whole struct and enable individual setters via`#[builder(setter)]`.

The types of skipped fields must implement `Default`.

```
#[derive(Builder)]
struct HiddenField {
    setter_present: u32,
    #[builder(setter(skip))]
    setter_skipped: u32,
}
```
Alternatively, you can use the more verbose form:

- `#[builder(setter(skip = true))]`
- `#[builder(setter(skip = false))]`

[§](https://docs.rs#custom-setters-skip-autogenerated-setters)Custom setters (skip autogenerated setters)

Similarly to `setter(skip)`, you can say that you will provide your own setter methods.
This simply suppresses the generation of the setter, leaving the field in the builder,
as `Option<T>`.

```
#[derive(Builder)]
struct SetterOptOut {
    #[builder(setter(custom))]
    custom_setter: u32,
}
impl SetterOptOutBuilder {
    fn custom_setter(&mut self, value: u32) {
        self.custom_setter = Some(value);
    }
}
```
Again, the more verbose form is accepted:

- `#[builder(setter(custom = true))]`
- `#[builder(setter(custom = false))]`

[§](https://docs.rs#setter-visibility)Setter Visibility

Setters are public by default. You can precede your struct (or field) with `#[builder(public)]`
to make this explicit.

Otherwise precede your struct (or field) with `#[builder(private)]` to opt into private
setters.

[§](https://docs.rs#generated-builder-struct-name)Generated builder struct name

By default, the builder struct for `struct Foo` is `FooBuilder`.
You can override this:

```
#[derive(Builder)]
#[builder(name = "FooConstructor")]
struct Foo { }
let foo: Foo = FooConstructor::default().build()?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#setter-nameprefix)Setter Name/Prefix

Setter methods are named after their corresponding field by default.

- You can customize the setter name via `#[builder(setter(name = "foo"))`.
- Alternatively you can set a prefix via `#[builder(setter(prefix = "xyz"))`, which will change the method name to`xyz_foo`if the field is named`foo`. Note that an underscore is inserted, since Rust favors snake case here.

Prefixes can also be defined on the struct level, but renames only work on fields. Renames take precedence over prefix definitions.

[§](https://docs.rs#generic-setters)Generic Setters

You can make each setter generic over the `Into`-trait. It’s as simple as adding
`#[builder(setter(into))]` to either a field or the whole struct.

```
#[derive(Builder, Debug, PartialEq)]
struct Lorem {
    #[builder(setter(into))]
    pub ipsum: String,
}
fn main() {
    // `"foo"` will be converted into a `String` automatically.
    let x = LoremBuilder::default().ipsum("foo").build().unwrap();
    assert_eq!(x, Lorem {
        ipsum: "foo".to_string(),
    });
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#setters-for-option)Setters for Option

You can avoid wrapping values in `Some(...)` for fields of type `Option<T>`. It’s as simple as adding
`#[builder(setter(strip_option))]` to either a single field or the whole struct.

```
#[derive(Builder, Debug, PartialEq)]
struct Lorem {
    #[builder(setter(into, strip_option))]
    pub ipsum: Option<String>,
    #[builder(setter(into, strip_option), default)]
    pub foo: Option<String>,
}
fn main() {
    // `"foo"` will be converted into a `String` automatically.
    let x = LoremBuilder::default().ipsum("foo").build().unwrap();
    assert_eq!(x, Lorem {
        ipsum: Some("foo".to_string()),
        foo: None
    });
}
```
If you want to set the value to None when unset, then enable `default` on this field (or do not use `strip_option`).

Limitation: only the `Option` type name is supported, not type alias nor `std::option::Option`.

[§](https://docs.rs#fallible-setters)Fallible Setters

Alongside the normal setter methods, you can expose fallible setters which are generic over
the `TryInto` trait. TryInto is similar to `Into` with the key distinction that the conversion
can fail, and therefore produces a `Result`.

You can only declare the `try_setter` attribute today if you’re targeting nightly, and you have
to add `#![feature(try_from)]` to your crate to use it.

```
#[derive(Builder, Debug, PartialEq)]
#[builder(try_setter, setter(into))]
struct Lorem {
    pub name: String,
    pub ipsum: u8,
}
#[derive(Builder, Debug, PartialEq)]
struct Ipsum {
    #[builder(try_setter, setter(into, name = "foo"))]
    pub dolor: u8,
}
fn main() {
   LoremBuilder::default()
       .try_ipsum(1u16).unwrap()
       .name("hello")
       .build()
       .expect("1 fits into a u8");
   IpsumBuilder::default()
       .try_foo(1u16).unwrap()
       .build()
       .expect("1 fits into a u8");
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#default-values)Default Values

You can define default values for each field via annotation by `#[builder(default = "...")]`,
where `...` stands for any Rust expression and must be string-escaped, e.g.

- `#[builder(default = "42")]`
- `#[builder(default)]`delegates to the- `Default`

The expression will be evaluated with each call to `build`.

```
#[derive(Builder, Debug, PartialEq)]
struct Lorem {
    #[builder(default = "42")]
    pub ipsum: u32,
}
fn main() {
    // If we don't set the field `ipsum`,
    let x = LoremBuilder::default().build().unwrap();
    // .. the custom default will be used for `ipsum`:
    assert_eq!(x, Lorem {
        ipsum: 42,
    });
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#tips-on-defaults)Tips on Defaults

- The `#[builder(default)]`annotation can be used on the struct level, too. Overrides are still possible.
- Delegate to a private helper method on `FooBuilder`for anything fancy. This way you will get*much better error diagnostics*from the rust compiler and it will be*much more readable*for other human beings. :-)
- Defaults will not work while using `#[builder(build_fn(skip))]`. In this case, you’ll need to handle default values yourself when converting from the builder, such as by using`.unwrap_or()`and`.unwrap_or_else()`.

```
struct Lorem {
    ipsum: String,
    // Custom defaults can delegate to helper methods
    // and pass errors to the enclosing `build()` method via `?`.
    #[builder(default = "self.default_dolor()?")]
    dolor: String,
}
impl LoremBuilder {
    // Private helper method with access to the builder struct.
    fn default_dolor(&self) -> Result<String, String> {
        match self.ipsum {
            Some(ref x) if x.chars().count() > 3 => Ok(format!("dolor {}", x)),
            _ => Err("ipsum must at least 3 chars to build dolor".to_string()),
        }
    }
}
```
You can even reference other fields, but you have to remember that the builder struct
will wrap every type in an Option ([as illustrated earlier](https://docs.rs#what-you-get)).

[§](https://docs.rs#generic-structs)Generic Structs

```
#[derive(Builder, Debug, PartialEq, Default, Clone)]
struct GenLorem<T: Clone> {
    ipsum: &'static str,
    dolor: T,
}
fn main() {
    let x = GenLoremBuilder::default().ipsum("sit").dolor(42).build().unwrap();
    assert_eq!(x, GenLorem { ipsum: "sit".into(), dolor: 42 });
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#build-method-customization)Build Method Customization

You can rename or suppress the auto-generated build method, leaving you free to implement
your own version. Suppression is done using `#[builder(build_fn(skip))]` at the struct level,
and renaming is done with `#[builder(build_fn(name = "YOUR_NAME"))]`.

Additionally if you want to make the build method private you can apply `#[builder(build_fn(private))]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#pre-build-validation)Pre-Build Validation

If you’re using the provided `build` method, you can declare
`#[builder(build_fn(validate = "path::to::fn"))]` to specify a validator function which gets
access to the builder before construction. The path does not need to be fully-qualified, and
will consider `use` statements made at module level. It must be accessible from the scope
where the target struct is declared.

The provided function must have the signature `(&FooBuilder) -> Result<_, String>`;
the `Ok` variant is not used by the `build` method.

```
#[derive(Builder, Debug, PartialEq)]
#[builder(build_fn(validate = "Self::validate"))]
struct Lorem {
    pub ipsum: u8,
}
impl LoremBuilder {
    /// Check that `Lorem` is putting in the right amount of effort.
    fn validate(&self) -> Result<(), String> {
        if let Some(ref ipsum) = self.ipsum {
            match *ipsum {
                i if i < 20 => Err("Try harder".to_string()),
                i if i > 100 => Err("You'll tire yourself out".to_string()),
                _ => Ok(())
            }
        } else {
            Ok(())
        }
    }
}
fn main() {
    // If we're trying too hard...
    let x = LoremBuilder::default().ipsum(120).build().unwrap_err();
    // .. the build will fail:
    assert_eq!(&x.to_string(), "You'll tire yourself out");
}
```
Note:

- Default values are applied *after*validation, and will therefore not be validated!

[§](https://docs.rs#additional-trait-derivations)Additional Trait Derivations

You can derive additional traits on the builder, including traits defined by other crates:

```
#[derive(Builder, Clone)]
#[builder(derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq))]
pub struct Lorem {
    foo: u8,
    bar: String,
}
fn main() {
   assert_eq!(LoremBuilder::default(), LoremBuilder::default());
}
```
Attributes declared for those traits are *not* forwarded to the fields on the builder.

[§](https://docs.rs#documentation-comments-and-attributes)Documentation Comments and Attributes

`#[derive(Builder)]` copies doc comments and attributes (`#[...]`) from your fields
to the according builder fields and setter-methods, if it is one of the following:

- `/// ...`
- `#[doc = ...]`
- `#[cfg(...)]`
- `#[allow(...)]`

The whitelisting minimizes interference with other custom attributes like those used by Serde, Diesel, or others.

```
#[derive(Builder)]
struct Lorem {
    /// `ipsum` may be any `String` (be creative).
    ipsum: String,
    #[doc = r"`dolor` is the estimated amount of work."]
    dolor: i32,
    // `#[derive(Builder)]` understands conditional compilation via cfg-attributes,
    // i.e. => "no field = no setter".
    #[cfg(target_os = "macos")]
    #[allow(non_snake_case)]
    Im_a_Mac: bool,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#pass-through-attributes)Pass-through Attributes

You can set attributes on elements of the builder using the `builder_*_attr` attributes:

- `builder_struct_attr`adds attributes after- `#[derive(...)]`on the builder struct.
- `builder_impl_attr`adds attributes on the- `impl`block
- `builder_field_attr`adds attributes to field declarations in the builder struct.
- `builder_setter_attr`adds attributes to the setter in the- `impl`block.

```
#[derive(Builder)]
#[builder(derive(serde::Serialize))]
#[builder_struct_attr(serde(rename_all = "camelCase"))]
struct Lorem {
    #[builder_field_attr(serde(rename="dolor"))]
    ipsum: String,
}
let mut show = LoremBuilder::default();
show.ipsum("sit".into());
assert_eq!(serde_json::to_string(&show).unwrap(), r#"{"dolor":"sit"}"#);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#error-return-type-from-autogenerated-build-function)Error return type from autogenerated `build` function

By default, `build` returns an autogenerated error type:

```
#[doc="Error type for LoremBuilder"]
#[derive(Debug)]
#[non_exhaustive]
pub enum LoremBuilderError { // where `LoremBuilder` is the name of the builder struct
    /// Uninitialized field
    UninitializedField(&'static str),
    /// Custom validation error
    ValidationError(String),
}
impl From<String> for LoremBuilderError {
    fn from(s: String) -> Self { Self::ValidationError(s) }
}
impl From<UninitializedFieldError> for LoremBuilderError { // ...
impl Display for LoremBuilderError { // ...
impl std::error::Error for LoremBuilderError {}
```
Alternatively, you can specify your own error type:

```
#[derive(Builder, Debug, PartialEq)]
#[builder(build_fn(error = "OurLoremError"))]
struct Lorem {
    pub ipsum: u32,
}
struct OurLoremError(String);
impl From<UninitializedFieldError> for OurLoremError {
    fn from(ufe: UninitializedFieldError) -> OurLoremError { OurLoremError(ufe.to_string()) }
}
let err: OurLoremError = LoremBuilder::default().build().unwrap_err();
assert_eq!(&err.0, "Field not initialized: ipsum");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#completely-custom-fields-in-the-builder)Completely custom fields in the builder

Instead of having an `Option`, you can have whatever type you like:

```
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Default, Builder, Clone)]
#[builder(derive(Debug, PartialEq))]
struct Lorem {
    #[builder(setter(into), field(ty = "u32"))]
    ipsum: u32,
    #[builder(field(ty = "String", build = "()"))]
    dolor: (),
    #[builder(field(ty = "&'static str", build = "self.amet.parse()?"))]
    amet: u32,
}
impl From<std::num::ParseIntError> for LoremBuilderError { // ...
let mut builder = LoremBuilder::default();
builder.ipsum(42u16).dolor("sit".into()).amet("12");
assert_eq!(builder, LoremBuilder { ipsum: 42, dolor: "sit".into(), amet: "12" });
let lorem = builder.build().unwrap();
assert_eq!(lorem, Lorem { ipsum: 42, dolor: (), amet: 12 });
```
The builder field type (`ty =`) must implement `Default`.

The argument to `build` must be a literal string containing Rust code for the contents of a block, which must evaluate to the type of the target field.
It may refer to the builder struct as `self`, use `?`, etc.

[§](https://docs.rs#no_std-support-on-nightly)`#![no_std]`

`#![no_std]`You can activate support for `#![no_std]` by adding `#[builder(no_std)]` to your struct
and `#![feature(alloc)] extern crate alloc` to your crate.

The latter requires the *nightly* toolchain.

[§](https://docs.rs#troubleshooting)Troubleshooting

[§](https://docs.rs#gotchas)Gotchas

- Tuple structs and unit structs are not supported as they have no field names.
- Generic setters introduce a type parameter `VALUE: Into<_>`. Therefore you can’t use`VALUE`as a type parameter on a generic struct in combination with generic setters.
- The `try_setter`attribute and`owned`builder pattern are not compatible in practice; an error during building will consume the builder, making it impossible to continue construction.
- When re-exporting the underlying struct under a different name, the auto-generated documentation will not match.
- If derive_builder depends on your crate, and vice versa, then a cyclic
dependency would occur. To break it you could try to depend on the
`derive_builder_core`

[§](https://docs.rs#report-issues-and-ideas)Report Issues and Ideas

If possible please try to provide the debugging info if you experience unexpected compilation errors (see above).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Uninitialized](https://docs.rs/struct.UninitializedFieldError.html)- Field - Error
- Runtime error when a `build()`method is called and one or more required fields do not have a value.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Builder](https://docs.rs/derive.Builder.html)
- Create a builder struct for the deriving struct.

# lib.rs - source

# derive_builder/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! Derive a builder for a struct
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! This crate implements the [builder pattern] for you.
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! Just apply `#[derive(Builder)]` to a struct `Foo`, and it will derive an additional
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! struct `FooBuilder` with **setter**-methods for all fields and a **build**-method
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! — the way you want it.
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//!
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! # Quick Start
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//!
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! Add `derive_builder` as a dependency to you `Cargo.toml`.
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//!
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! ## What you write
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! ```rust
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! use derive_builder::Builder;
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! #[derive(Builder)]
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! struct Lorem {
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//!     ipsum: u32,
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!     // ..
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! }
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! # fn main() {}
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! ```
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//!
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! ## What you get
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//!
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! ```rust
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! # use derive_builder::{Builder, UninitializedFieldError};
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! #
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! # struct Lorem {
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! #     ipsum: u32,
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! # }
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! # fn main() {}
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! #
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! #[derive(Clone, Default)]
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! struct LoremBuilder {
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//!     ipsum: Option<u32>,
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! }
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! # // bodge for testing:
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! # type LoremBuilderError = UninitializedFieldError;
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//!
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! #[allow(dead_code)]
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! impl LoremBuilder {
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!     pub fn ipsum(&mut self, value: u32) -> &mut Self {
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//!         let mut new = self;
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!         new.ipsum = Some(value);
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!         new
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!     }
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!     fn build(&self) -> Result<Lorem, LoremBuilderError> {
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!         Ok(Lorem {
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!             ipsum: Clone::clone(self.ipsum
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//!                 .as_ref()
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!                 .ok_or(LoremBuilderError::from(UninitializedFieldError::new("ipsum")))?),
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//!         })
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!     }
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! }
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! ```
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//!
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! By default all generated setter-methods take and return `&mut self`
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! (aka _non-consuming_ builder pattern). Accordingly, the build method also takes a
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! reference by default.
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//!
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! You can easily opt into different patterns and control many other aspects.
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! The build method returns `Result<T, E>`, where `T` is the struct you started with
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! and E is a generated builder error type.
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! It returns `Err` if you didn't initialize all fields and no default values were
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! provided.
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//!
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! # Builder Patterns
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//!
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! Let's look again at the example above. You can now build structs like this:
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! ```rust
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! # use derive_builder::Builder;
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! # #[derive(Builder)] struct Lorem { ipsum: u32 }
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! # fn try_main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! let x: Lorem = LoremBuilder::default().ipsum(42).build()?;
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! # Ok(())
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! # } fn main() { try_main().unwrap(); }
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! ```
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//!
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! Ok, _chaining_ method calls is nice, but what if `ipsum(42)` should only happen if `geek = true`?
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//!
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! So let's make this call conditional
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! ```rust
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! # use derive_builder::Builder;
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! # #[derive(Builder)] struct Lorem { ipsum: u32 }
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! # fn try_main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! # let geek = true;
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! let mut builder = LoremBuilder::default();
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! if geek {
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//!     builder.ipsum(42);
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! }
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! let x: Lorem = builder.build()?;
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! # Ok(())
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! # } fn main() { try_main().unwrap(); }
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! ```
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//!
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! Now it comes in handy that our setter methods take and return mutable references. Otherwise
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! we would need to write something more clumsy like `builder = builder.ipsum(42)` to reassign
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! the return value each time we have to call a setter conditionally.
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//!
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! Setters with mutable references are therefore a convenient default for the builder
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! pattern in Rust.
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//!
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! But this is a free world and the choice is still yours!
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//!
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! ## Owned, aka Consuming
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//!
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! Precede your struct (or field) with `#[builder(pattern = "owned")]` to opt into this pattern.
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! Builders generated with this pattern do not automatically derive `Clone`, which allows builders
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! to be generated for structs with fields that do not derive `Clone`.
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//!
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! * Setters take and return `self`.
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! * PRO: Setter calls and final build method can be chained.
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! * CON: If you don't chain your calls, you have to create a reference to each return value,
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//!   e.g. `builder = builder.ipsum(42)`.
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//!
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//! ## Mutable, aka Non-Consuming (recommended)
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//!
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//! This pattern is recommended and active by default if you don't specify anything else.
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//! You can precede your struct (or field) with `#[builder(pattern = "mutable")]`
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! to make this choice explicit.
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//!
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! * Setters take and return `&mut self`.
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//! * PRO: Setter calls and final build method can be chained.
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! * CON: The build method must clone or copy data to create something owned out of a
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//!   mutable reference. Otherwise it could not be used in a chain. **(*)**
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//!
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//! ## Immutable
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//!
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//! Precede your struct (or field) with `#[builder(pattern = "immutable")]` to opt into this pattern.
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//!
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//! * Setters take and return `&self`.
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! * PRO: Setter calls and final build method can be chained.
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! * CON: If you don't chain your calls, you have to create a reference to each return value,
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//!   e.g. `builder = builder.ipsum(42)`.
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! * CON: The build method _and each setter_ must clone or copy data to create something owned
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//!   out of a reference. **(*)**
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//!
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//! ## (*) Performance Considerations
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//!
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! Luckily Rust is clever enough to optimize these clone-calls away in release builds
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//! for your every-day use cases. Thats quite a safe bet - we checked this for you. ;-)
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! Switching to consuming signatures (=`self`) is unlikely to give you any performance
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//! gain, but very likely to restrict your API for non-chained use cases.
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//!
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//! # More Features
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//!
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! ## Hidden Fields
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//!
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//! You can hide fields by skipping their setters on (and presence in) the builder struct.
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//!
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! - Opt-out — skip setters via `#[builder(setter(skip))]` on individual fields.
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//! - Opt-in — set `#[builder(setter(skip))]` on the whole struct
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//!   and enable individual setters via `#[builder(setter)]`.
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//!
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//! The types of skipped fields must implement `Default`.
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//!
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//! ```rust
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//! # use derive_builder::Builder;
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//! #
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//! #[derive(Builder)]
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//! struct HiddenField {
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//!     setter_present: u32,
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//!     #[builder(setter(skip))]
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//!     setter_skipped: u32,
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//! }
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//! # fn main() {}
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//! ```
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//!
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//! Alternatively, you can use the more verbose form:
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//!
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//! - `#[builder(setter(skip = true))]`
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//! - `#[builder(setter(skip = false))]`
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//!
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//! ## Custom setters (skip autogenerated setters)
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//!
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//! Similarly to `setter(skip)`, you can say that you will provide your own setter methods.
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//! This simply suppresses the generation of the setter, leaving the field in the builder,
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//! as `Option<T>`.
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//!
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//! ```rust
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//! # use derive_builder::Builder;
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//! #
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//! #[derive(Builder)]
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//! struct SetterOptOut {
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//!     #[builder(setter(custom))]
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//!     custom_setter: u32,
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//! }
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//! impl SetterOptOutBuilder {
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//!     fn custom_setter(&mut self, value: u32) {
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//!         self.custom_setter = Some(value);
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//!     }
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//! }
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//! # fn main() {}
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//! ```
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//!
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//! Again, the more verbose form is accepted:
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//!
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//! - `#[builder(setter(custom = true))]`
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//! - `#[builder(setter(custom = false))]`
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//!
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//! ## Setter Visibility
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//!
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//! Setters are public by default. You can precede your struct (or field) with `#[builder(public)]`
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//! to make this explicit.
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//!
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//! Otherwise precede your struct (or field) with `#[builder(private)]` to opt into private
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! setters.
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//!
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//! ## Generated builder struct name
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//!
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//! By default, the builder struct for `struct Foo` is `FooBuilder`.
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//! You can override this:
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//!
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//! ```rust
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//! # use derive_builder::Builder;
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//! #
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//! #[derive(Builder)]
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//! #[builder(name = "FooConstructor")]
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//! struct Foo { }
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//!
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//! # fn main() -> Result<(), FooConstructorError> {
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//! let foo: Foo = FooConstructor::default().build()?;
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//! # Ok(())
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//! # }
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//! ```
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//!
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//! ## Setter Name/Prefix
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//!
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//! Setter methods are named after their corresponding field by default.
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//!
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//! - You can customize the setter name via `#[builder(setter(name = "foo"))`.
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//! - Alternatively you can set a prefix via `#[builder(setter(prefix = "xyz"))`, which will change
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//!   the method name to `xyz_foo` if the field is named `foo`. Note that an underscore is
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//!   inserted, since Rust favors snake case here.
[241](https://docs.rs#241)//!
[242](https://docs.rs#242)//! Prefixes can also be defined on the struct level, but renames only work on fields. Renames
[243](https://docs.rs#243)//! take precedence over prefix definitions.
[244](https://docs.rs#244)//!
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//! ## Generic Setters
[246](https://docs.rs#246)//!
[247](https://docs.rs#247)//! You can make each setter generic over the `Into`-trait. It's as simple as adding
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//! `#[builder(setter(into))]` to either a field or the whole struct.
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//!
[250](https://docs.rs#250)//! ```rust
[251](https://docs.rs#251)//! # use derive_builder::Builder;
[252](https://docs.rs#252)//! #
[253](https://docs.rs#253)//! #[derive(Builder, Debug, PartialEq)]
[254](https://docs.rs#254)//! struct Lorem {
[255](https://docs.rs#255)//!     #[builder(setter(into))]
[256](https://docs.rs#256)//!     pub ipsum: String,
[257](https://docs.rs#257)//! }
[258](https://docs.rs#258)//!
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//! fn main() {
[260](https://docs.rs#260)//!     // `"foo"` will be converted into a `String` automatically.
[261](https://docs.rs#261)//!     let x = LoremBuilder::default().ipsum("foo").build().unwrap();
[262](https://docs.rs#262)//!
[263](https://docs.rs#263)//!     assert_eq!(x, Lorem {
[264](https://docs.rs#264)//!         ipsum: "foo".to_string(),
[265](https://docs.rs#265)//!     });
[266](https://docs.rs#266)//! }
[267](https://docs.rs#267)//! ```
[268](https://docs.rs#268)//!
[269](https://docs.rs#269)//! ## Setters for Option
[270](https://docs.rs#270)//!
[271](https://docs.rs#271)//! You can avoid wrapping values in `Some(...)` for fields of type `Option<T>`. It's as simple as adding
[272](https://docs.rs#272)//! `#[builder(setter(strip_option))]` to either a single field or the whole struct.
[273](https://docs.rs#273)//!
[274](https://docs.rs#274)//! ```rust
[275](https://docs.rs#275)//! # use derive_builder::Builder;
[276](https://docs.rs#276)//! #
[277](https://docs.rs#277)//! #[derive(Builder, Debug, PartialEq)]
[278](https://docs.rs#278)//! struct Lorem {
[279](https://docs.rs#279)//!     #[builder(setter(into, strip_option))]
[280](https://docs.rs#280)//!     pub ipsum: Option<String>,
[281](https://docs.rs#281)//!     #[builder(setter(into, strip_option), default)]
[282](https://docs.rs#282)//!     pub foo: Option<String>,
[283](https://docs.rs#283)//! }
[284](https://docs.rs#284)//!
[285](https://docs.rs#285)//! fn main() {
[286](https://docs.rs#286)//!     // `"foo"` will be converted into a `String` automatically.
[287](https://docs.rs#287)//!     let x = LoremBuilder::default().ipsum("foo").build().unwrap();
[288](https://docs.rs#288)//!
[289](https://docs.rs#289)//!     assert_eq!(x, Lorem {
[290](https://docs.rs#290)//!         ipsum: Some("foo".to_string()),
[291](https://docs.rs#291)//!         foo: None
[292](https://docs.rs#292)//!     });
[293](https://docs.rs#293)//! }
[294](https://docs.rs#294)//! ```
[295](https://docs.rs#295)//! If you want to set the value to None when unset, then enable `default` on this field (or do not use `strip_option`).
[296](https://docs.rs#296)//!
[297](https://docs.rs#297)//! Limitation: only the `Option` type name is supported, not type alias nor `std::option::Option`.
[298](https://docs.rs#298)//!
[299](https://docs.rs#299)//! ## Fallible Setters
[300](https://docs.rs#300)//!
[301](https://docs.rs#301)//! Alongside the normal setter methods, you can expose fallible setters which are generic over
[302](https://docs.rs#302)//! the `TryInto` trait. TryInto is similar to `Into` with the key distinction that the conversion
[303](https://docs.rs#303)//! can fail, and therefore produces a `Result`.
[304](https://docs.rs#304)//!
[305](https://docs.rs#305)//! You can only declare the `try_setter` attribute today if you're targeting nightly, and you have
[306](https://docs.rs#306)//! to add `#![feature(try_from)]` to your crate to use it.
[307](https://docs.rs#307)//!
[308](https://docs.rs#308)//! ```rust
[309](https://docs.rs#309)//! # use derive_builder::Builder;
[310](https://docs.rs#310)//! #[derive(Builder, Debug, PartialEq)]
[311](https://docs.rs#311)//! #[builder(try_setter, setter(into))]
[312](https://docs.rs#312)//! struct Lorem {
[313](https://docs.rs#313)//!     pub name: String,
[314](https://docs.rs#314)//!     pub ipsum: u8,
[315](https://docs.rs#315)//! }
[316](https://docs.rs#316)//!
[317](https://docs.rs#317)//! #[derive(Builder, Debug, PartialEq)]
[318](https://docs.rs#318)//! struct Ipsum {
[319](https://docs.rs#319)//!     #[builder(try_setter, setter(into, name = "foo"))]
[320](https://docs.rs#320)//!     pub dolor: u8,
[321](https://docs.rs#321)//! }
[322](https://docs.rs#322)//!
[323](https://docs.rs#323)//! fn main() {
[324](https://docs.rs#324)//!    LoremBuilder::default()
[325](https://docs.rs#325)//!        .try_ipsum(1u16).unwrap()
[326](https://docs.rs#326)//!        .name("hello")
[327](https://docs.rs#327)//!        .build()
[328](https://docs.rs#328)//!        .expect("1 fits into a u8");
[329](https://docs.rs#329)//!
[330](https://docs.rs#330)//!    IpsumBuilder::default()
[331](https://docs.rs#331)//!        .try_foo(1u16).unwrap()
[332](https://docs.rs#332)//!        .build()
[333](https://docs.rs#333)//!        .expect("1 fits into a u8");
[334](https://docs.rs#334)//! }
[335](https://docs.rs#335)//! ```
[336](https://docs.rs#336)//!
[337](https://docs.rs#337)//! ## Default Values
[338](https://docs.rs#338)//!
[339](https://docs.rs#339)//! You can define default values for each field via annotation by `#[builder(default = "...")]`,
[340](https://docs.rs#340)//! where `...` stands for any Rust expression and must be string-escaped, e.g.
[341](https://docs.rs#341)//!
[342](https://docs.rs#342)//! * `#[builder(default = "42")]`
[343](https://docs.rs#343)//! * `#[builder(default)]` delegates to the [`Default`] trait of the base type.
[344](https://docs.rs#344)//!
[345](https://docs.rs#345)//! The expression will be evaluated with each call to `build`.
[346](https://docs.rs#346)//!
[347](https://docs.rs#347)//! ```rust
[348](https://docs.rs#348)//! # use derive_builder::Builder;
[349](https://docs.rs#349)//! #
[350](https://docs.rs#350)//! #[derive(Builder, Debug, PartialEq)]
[351](https://docs.rs#351)//! struct Lorem {
[352](https://docs.rs#352)//!     #[builder(default = "42")]
[353](https://docs.rs#353)//!     pub ipsum: u32,
[354](https://docs.rs#354)//! }
[355](https://docs.rs#355)//!
[356](https://docs.rs#356)//! fn main() {
[357](https://docs.rs#357)//!     // If we don't set the field `ipsum`,
[358](https://docs.rs#358)//!     let x = LoremBuilder::default().build().unwrap();
[359](https://docs.rs#359)//!
[360](https://docs.rs#360)//!     // .. the custom default will be used for `ipsum`:
[361](https://docs.rs#361)//!     assert_eq!(x, Lorem {
[362](https://docs.rs#362)//!         ipsum: 42,
[363](https://docs.rs#363)//!     });
[364](https://docs.rs#364)//! }
[365](https://docs.rs#365)//! ```
[366](https://docs.rs#366)//!
[367](https://docs.rs#367)//! ### Tips on Defaults
[368](https://docs.rs#368)//!
[369](https://docs.rs#369)//! * The `#[builder(default)]` annotation can be used on the struct level, too. Overrides are
[370](https://docs.rs#370)//!   still possible.
[371](https://docs.rs#371)//! * Delegate to a private helper method on `FooBuilder` for anything fancy. This way
[372](https://docs.rs#372)//!   you will get _much better error diagnostics_ from the rust compiler and it will be _much
[373](https://docs.rs#373)//!   more readable_ for other human beings. :-)
[374](https://docs.rs#374)//! * Defaults will not work while using `#[builder(build_fn(skip))]`. In this case, you'll
[375](https://docs.rs#375)//!   need to handle default values yourself when converting from the builder, such as by
[376](https://docs.rs#376)//!   using `.unwrap_or()` and `.unwrap_or_else()`.
[377](https://docs.rs#377)//!
[378](https://docs.rs#378)//! [`Default`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/default/trait.Default.html
[379](https://docs.rs#379)//!
[380](https://docs.rs#380)//! ```rust
[381](https://docs.rs#381)//! # use derive_builder::Builder;
[382](https://docs.rs#382)//! #
[383](https://docs.rs#383)//! # #[derive(Builder, PartialEq, Debug)]
[384](https://docs.rs#384)//! struct Lorem {
[385](https://docs.rs#385)//!     ipsum: String,
[386](https://docs.rs#386)//!     // Custom defaults can delegate to helper methods
[387](https://docs.rs#387)//!     // and pass errors to the enclosing `build()` method via `?`.
[388](https://docs.rs#388)//!     #[builder(default = "self.default_dolor()?")]
[389](https://docs.rs#389)//!     dolor: String,
[390](https://docs.rs#390)//! }
[391](https://docs.rs#391)//!
[392](https://docs.rs#392)//! impl LoremBuilder {
[393](https://docs.rs#393)//!     // Private helper method with access to the builder struct.
[394](https://docs.rs#394)//!     fn default_dolor(&self) -> Result<String, String> {
[395](https://docs.rs#395)//!         match self.ipsum {
[396](https://docs.rs#396)//!             Some(ref x) if x.chars().count() > 3 => Ok(format!("dolor {}", x)),
[397](https://docs.rs#397)//!             _ => Err("ipsum must at least 3 chars to build dolor".to_string()),
[398](https://docs.rs#398)//!         }
[399](https://docs.rs#399)//!     }
[400](https://docs.rs#400)//! }
[401](https://docs.rs#401)//!
[402](https://docs.rs#402)//! # fn main() {
[403](https://docs.rs#403)//! #     let x = LoremBuilder::default()
[404](https://docs.rs#404)//! #         .ipsum("ipsum".to_string())
[405](https://docs.rs#405)//! #         .build()
[406](https://docs.rs#406)//! #         .unwrap();
[407](https://docs.rs#407)//! #
[408](https://docs.rs#408)//! #     assert_eq!(x, Lorem {
[409](https://docs.rs#409)//! #         ipsum: "ipsum".to_string(),
[410](https://docs.rs#410)//! #         dolor: "dolor ipsum".to_string(),
[411](https://docs.rs#411)//! #     });
[412](https://docs.rs#412)//! # }
[413](https://docs.rs#413)//! ```
[414](https://docs.rs#414)//!
[415](https://docs.rs#415)//! You can even reference other fields, but you have to remember that the builder struct
[416](https://docs.rs#416)//! will wrap every type in an Option ([as illustrated earlier](#what-you-get)).
[417](https://docs.rs#417)//!
[418](https://docs.rs#418)//! ## Generic Structs
[419](https://docs.rs#419)//!
[420](https://docs.rs#420)//! ```rust
[421](https://docs.rs#421)//! # use derive_builder::Builder;
[422](https://docs.rs#422)//! #
[423](https://docs.rs#423)//! #[derive(Builder, Debug, PartialEq, Default, Clone)]
[424](https://docs.rs#424)//! struct GenLorem<T: Clone> {
[425](https://docs.rs#425)//!     ipsum: &'static str,
[426](https://docs.rs#426)//!     dolor: T,
[427](https://docs.rs#427)//! }
[428](https://docs.rs#428)//!
[429](https://docs.rs#429)//! fn main() {
[430](https://docs.rs#430)//!     let x = GenLoremBuilder::default().ipsum("sit").dolor(42).build().unwrap();
[431](https://docs.rs#431)//!     assert_eq!(x, GenLorem { ipsum: "sit".into(), dolor: 42 });
[432](https://docs.rs#432)//! }
[433](https://docs.rs#433)//! ```
[434](https://docs.rs#434)//!
[435](https://docs.rs#435)//! ## Build Method Customization
[436](https://docs.rs#436)//!
[437](https://docs.rs#437)//! You can rename or suppress the auto-generated build method, leaving you free to implement
[438](https://docs.rs#438)//! your own version. Suppression is done using `#[builder(build_fn(skip))]` at the struct level,
[439](https://docs.rs#439)//! and renaming is done with `#[builder(build_fn(name = "YOUR_NAME"))]`.
[440](https://docs.rs#440)//!
[441](https://docs.rs#441)//! Additionally if you want to make the build method private you can apply `#[builder(build_fn(private))]`.
[442](https://docs.rs#442)//!
[443](https://docs.rs#443)//! ## Pre-Build Validation
[444](https://docs.rs#444)//!
[445](https://docs.rs#445)//! If you're using the provided `build` method, you can declare
[446](https://docs.rs#446)//! `#[builder(build_fn(validate = "path::to::fn"))]` to specify a validator function which gets
[447](https://docs.rs#447)//! access to the builder before construction. The path does not need to be fully-qualified, and
[448](https://docs.rs#448)//! will consider `use` statements made at module level. It must be accessible from the scope
[449](https://docs.rs#449)//! where the target struct is declared.
[450](https://docs.rs#450)//!
[451](https://docs.rs#451)//! The provided function must have the signature `(&FooBuilder) -> Result<_, String>`;
[452](https://docs.rs#452)//! the `Ok` variant is not used by the `build` method.
[453](https://docs.rs#453)//!
[454](https://docs.rs#454)//! ```rust
[455](https://docs.rs#455)//! # use derive_builder::Builder;
[456](https://docs.rs#456)//! #
[457](https://docs.rs#457)//! #[derive(Builder, Debug, PartialEq)]
[458](https://docs.rs#458)//! #[builder(build_fn(validate = "Self::validate"))]
[459](https://docs.rs#459)//! struct Lorem {
[460](https://docs.rs#460)//!     pub ipsum: u8,
[461](https://docs.rs#461)//! }
[462](https://docs.rs#462)//!
[463](https://docs.rs#463)//! impl LoremBuilder {
[464](https://docs.rs#464)//!     /// Check that `Lorem` is putting in the right amount of effort.
[465](https://docs.rs#465)//!     fn validate(&self) -> Result<(), String> {
[466](https://docs.rs#466)//!         if let Some(ref ipsum) = self.ipsum {
[467](https://docs.rs#467)//!             match *ipsum {
[468](https://docs.rs#468)//!                 i if i < 20 => Err("Try harder".to_string()),
[469](https://docs.rs#469)//!                 i if i > 100 => Err("You'll tire yourself out".to_string()),
[470](https://docs.rs#470)//!                 _ => Ok(())
[471](https://docs.rs#471)//!             }
[472](https://docs.rs#472)//!         } else {
[473](https://docs.rs#473)//!             Ok(())
[474](https://docs.rs#474)//!         }
[475](https://docs.rs#475)//!     }
[476](https://docs.rs#476)//! }
[477](https://docs.rs#477)//!
[478](https://docs.rs#478)//! fn main() {
[479](https://docs.rs#479)//!     // If we're trying too hard...
[480](https://docs.rs#480)//!     let x = LoremBuilder::default().ipsum(120).build().unwrap_err();
[481](https://docs.rs#481)//!
[482](https://docs.rs#482)//!     // .. the build will fail:
[483](https://docs.rs#483)//!     assert_eq!(&x.to_string(), "You'll tire yourself out");
[484](https://docs.rs#484)//! }
[485](https://docs.rs#485)//! ```
[486](https://docs.rs#486)//!
[487](https://docs.rs#487)//! Note:
[488](https://docs.rs#488)//! * Default values are applied _after_ validation, and will therefore not be validated!
[489](https://docs.rs#489)//!
[490](https://docs.rs#490)//! ## Additional Trait Derivations
[491](https://docs.rs#491)//!
[492](https://docs.rs#492)//! You can derive additional traits on the builder, including traits defined by other crates:
[493](https://docs.rs#493)//!
[494](https://docs.rs#494)//! ```rust
[495](https://docs.rs#495)//! # use derive_builder::Builder;
[496](https://docs.rs#496)//! #
[497](https://docs.rs#497)//! #[derive(Builder, Clone)]
[498](https://docs.rs#498)//! #[builder(derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq))]
[499](https://docs.rs#499)//! pub struct Lorem {
[500](https://docs.rs#500)//!     foo: u8,
[501](https://docs.rs#501)//!     bar: String,
[502](https://docs.rs#502)//! }
[503](https://docs.rs#503)//!
[504](https://docs.rs#504)//! fn main() {
[505](https://docs.rs#505)//!    assert_eq!(LoremBuilder::default(), LoremBuilder::default());
[506](https://docs.rs#506)//! }
[507](https://docs.rs#507)//! ```
[508](https://docs.rs#508)//!
[509](https://docs.rs#509)//! Attributes declared for those traits are _not_ forwarded to the fields on the builder.
[510](https://docs.rs#510)//!
[511](https://docs.rs#511)//! ## Documentation Comments and Attributes
[512](https://docs.rs#512)//!
[513](https://docs.rs#513)//! `#[derive(Builder)]` copies doc comments and attributes (`#[...]`) from your fields
[514](https://docs.rs#514)//! to the according builder fields and setter-methods, if it is one of the following:
[515](https://docs.rs#515)//!
[516](https://docs.rs#516)//! * `/// ...`
[517](https://docs.rs#517)//! * `#[doc = ...]`
[518](https://docs.rs#518)//! * `#[cfg(...)]`
[519](https://docs.rs#519)//! * `#[allow(...)]`
[520](https://docs.rs#520)//!
[521](https://docs.rs#521)//! The whitelisting minimizes interference with other custom attributes like
[522](https://docs.rs#522)//! those used by Serde, Diesel, or others.
[523](https://docs.rs#523)//!
[524](https://docs.rs#524)//! ```rust
[525](https://docs.rs#525)//! # use derive_builder::Builder;
[526](https://docs.rs#526)//! #
[527](https://docs.rs#527)//! #[derive(Builder)]
[528](https://docs.rs#528)//! struct Lorem {
[529](https://docs.rs#529)//!     /// `ipsum` may be any `String` (be creative).
[530](https://docs.rs#530)//!     ipsum: String,
[531](https://docs.rs#531)//!     #[doc = r"`dolor` is the estimated amount of work."]
[532](https://docs.rs#532)//!     dolor: i32,
[533](https://docs.rs#533)//!     // `#[derive(Builder)]` understands conditional compilation via cfg-attributes,
[534](https://docs.rs#534)//!     // i.e. => "no field = no setter".
[535](https://docs.rs#535)//!     #[cfg(target_os = "macos")]
[536](https://docs.rs#536)//!     #[allow(non_snake_case)]
[537](https://docs.rs#537)//!     Im_a_Mac: bool,
[538](https://docs.rs#538)//! }
[539](https://docs.rs#539)//! # fn main() {}
[540](https://docs.rs#540)//! ```
[541](https://docs.rs#541)//!
[542](https://docs.rs#542)//! ### Pass-through Attributes
[543](https://docs.rs#543)//!
[544](https://docs.rs#544)//! You can set attributes on elements of the builder using the `builder_*_attr` attributes:
[545](https://docs.rs#545)//!
[546](https://docs.rs#546)//! - `builder_struct_attr` adds attributes after `#[derive(...)]` on the builder struct.
[547](https://docs.rs#547)//! - `builder_impl_attr` adds attributes on the `impl` block
[548](https://docs.rs#548)//! - `builder_field_attr` adds attributes to field declarations in the builder struct.
[549](https://docs.rs#549)//! - `builder_setter_attr` adds attributes to the setter in the `impl` block.
[550](https://docs.rs#550)//!
[551](https://docs.rs#551)//! ```rust
[552](https://docs.rs#552)//! # use derive_builder::Builder;
[553](https://docs.rs#553)//! #
[554](https://docs.rs#554)//! #[derive(Builder)]
[555](https://docs.rs#555)//! #[builder(derive(serde::Serialize))]
[556](https://docs.rs#556)//! #[builder_struct_attr(serde(rename_all = "camelCase"))]
[557](https://docs.rs#557)//! struct Lorem {
[558](https://docs.rs#558)//!     #[builder_field_attr(serde(rename="dolor"))]
[559](https://docs.rs#559)//!     ipsum: String,
[560](https://docs.rs#560)//! }
[561](https://docs.rs#561)//!
[562](https://docs.rs#562)//! # fn main() {
[563](https://docs.rs#563)//! let mut show = LoremBuilder::default();
[564](https://docs.rs#564)//! show.ipsum("sit".into());
[565](https://docs.rs#565)//! assert_eq!(serde_json::to_string(&show).unwrap(), r#"{"dolor":"sit"}"#);
[566](https://docs.rs#566)//! # }
[567](https://docs.rs#567)//! ```
[568](https://docs.rs#568)//!
[569](https://docs.rs#569)//! # Error return type from autogenerated `build` function
[570](https://docs.rs#570)//!
[571](https://docs.rs#571)//! By default, `build` returns an autogenerated error type:
[572](https://docs.rs#572)//!
[573](https://docs.rs#573)//! ```rust
[574](https://docs.rs#574)//! # use derive_builder::UninitializedFieldError;
[575](https://docs.rs#575)//! # use std::fmt::{self, Display};
[576](https://docs.rs#576)//! #
[577](https://docs.rs#577)//! #[doc="Error type for LoremBuilder"]
[578](https://docs.rs#578)//! #[derive(Debug)]
[579](https://docs.rs#579)//! #[non_exhaustive]
[580](https://docs.rs#580)//! pub enum LoremBuilderError { // where `LoremBuilder` is the name of the builder struct
[581](https://docs.rs#581)//!     /// Uninitialized field
[582](https://docs.rs#582)//!     UninitializedField(&'static str),
[583](https://docs.rs#583)//!     /// Custom validation error
[584](https://docs.rs#584)//!     ValidationError(String),
[585](https://docs.rs#585)//! }
[586](https://docs.rs#586)//!
[587](https://docs.rs#587)//! impl From<String> for LoremBuilderError {
[588](https://docs.rs#588)//!     fn from(s: String) -> Self { Self::ValidationError(s) }
[589](https://docs.rs#589)//! }
[590](https://docs.rs#590)//! impl From<UninitializedFieldError> for LoremBuilderError { // ...
[591](https://docs.rs#591)//! # fn from(s: UninitializedFieldError) -> Self { todo!() } }
[592](https://docs.rs#592)//! impl Display for LoremBuilderError { // ...
[593](https://docs.rs#593)//! # fn fmt(&self, _: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result { todo!() } }
[594](https://docs.rs#594)//! impl std::error::Error for LoremBuilderError {}
[595](https://docs.rs#595)//! ```
[596](https://docs.rs#596)//!
[597](https://docs.rs#597)//! Alternatively, you can specify your own error type:
[598](https://docs.rs#598)//! ```rust
[599](https://docs.rs#599)//! # use derive_builder::{Builder, UninitializedFieldError};
[600](https://docs.rs#600)//! #
[601](https://docs.rs#601)//! #[derive(Builder, Debug, PartialEq)]
[602](https://docs.rs#602)//! #[builder(build_fn(error = "OurLoremError"))]
[603](https://docs.rs#603)//! struct Lorem {
[604](https://docs.rs#604)//!     pub ipsum: u32,
[605](https://docs.rs#605)//! }
[606](https://docs.rs#606)//!
[607](https://docs.rs#607)//! struct OurLoremError(String);
[608](https://docs.rs#608)//!
[609](https://docs.rs#609)//! impl From<UninitializedFieldError> for OurLoremError {
[610](https://docs.rs#610)//!     fn from(ufe: UninitializedFieldError) -> OurLoremError { OurLoremError(ufe.to_string()) }
[611](https://docs.rs#611)//! }
[612](https://docs.rs#612)//!
[613](https://docs.rs#613)//! # fn main() {
[614](https://docs.rs#614)//! let err: OurLoremError = LoremBuilder::default().build().unwrap_err();
[615](https://docs.rs#615)//! assert_eq!(&err.0, "Field not initialized: ipsum");
[616](https://docs.rs#616)//! # }
[617](https://docs.rs#617)//! ```
[618](https://docs.rs#618)//!
[619](https://docs.rs#619)//! # Completely custom fields in the builder
[620](https://docs.rs#620)//!
[621](https://docs.rs#621)//! Instead of having an `Option`, you can have whatever type you like:
[622](https://docs.rs#622)//!
[623](https://docs.rs#623)//! ```rust
[624](https://docs.rs#624)//! # use derive_builder::Builder;
[625](https://docs.rs#625)//! #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Default, Builder, Clone)]
[626](https://docs.rs#626)//! #[builder(derive(Debug, PartialEq))]
[627](https://docs.rs#627)//! struct Lorem {
[628](https://docs.rs#628)//!     #[builder(setter(into), field(ty = "u32"))]
[629](https://docs.rs#629)//!     ipsum: u32,
[630](https://docs.rs#630)//!
[631](https://docs.rs#631)//!     #[builder(field(ty = "String", build = "()"))]
[632](https://docs.rs#632)//!     dolor: (),
[633](https://docs.rs#633)//!
[634](https://docs.rs#634)//!     #[builder(field(ty = "&'static str", build = "self.amet.parse()?"))]
[635](https://docs.rs#635)//!     amet: u32,
[636](https://docs.rs#636)//! }
[637](https://docs.rs#637)//!
[638](https://docs.rs#638)//! impl From<std::num::ParseIntError> for LoremBuilderError { // ...
[639](https://docs.rs#639)//! #     fn from(e: std::num::ParseIntError) -> LoremBuilderError {
[640](https://docs.rs#640)//! #         e.to_string().into()
[641](https://docs.rs#641)//! #     }
[642](https://docs.rs#642)//! # }
[643](https://docs.rs#643)//!
[644](https://docs.rs#644)//! # fn main() {
[645](https://docs.rs#645)//! let mut builder = LoremBuilder::default();
[646](https://docs.rs#646)//! builder.ipsum(42u16).dolor("sit".into()).amet("12");
[647](https://docs.rs#647)//! assert_eq!(builder, LoremBuilder { ipsum: 42, dolor: "sit".into(), amet: "12" });
[648](https://docs.rs#648)//! let lorem = builder.build().unwrap();
[649](https://docs.rs#649)//! assert_eq!(lorem, Lorem { ipsum: 42, dolor: (), amet: 12 });
[650](https://docs.rs#650)//! # }
[651](https://docs.rs#651)//! ```
[652](https://docs.rs#652)//!
[653](https://docs.rs#653)//! The builder field type (`ty =`) must implement `Default`.
[654](https://docs.rs#654)//!
[655](https://docs.rs#655)//! The argument to `build` must be a literal string containing Rust code for the contents of a block, which must evaluate to the type of the target field.
[656](https://docs.rs#656)//! It may refer to the builder struct as `self`, use `?`, etc.
[657](https://docs.rs#657)//!
[658](https://docs.rs#658)//! # **`#![no_std]`** Support (on Nightly)
[659](https://docs.rs#659)//!
[660](https://docs.rs#660)//! You can activate support for `#![no_std]` by adding `#[builder(no_std)]` to your struct
[661](https://docs.rs#661)//! and `#![feature(alloc)] extern crate alloc` to your crate.
[662](https://docs.rs#662)//!
[663](https://docs.rs#663)//! The latter requires the _nightly_ toolchain.
[664](https://docs.rs#664)//!
[665](https://docs.rs#665)//! # Troubleshooting
[666](https://docs.rs#666)//!
[667](https://docs.rs#667)//! ## Gotchas
[668](https://docs.rs#668)//!
[669](https://docs.rs#669)//! - Tuple structs and unit structs are not supported as they have no field
[670](https://docs.rs#670)//!   names.
[671](https://docs.rs#671)//! - Generic setters introduce a type parameter `VALUE: Into<_>`. Therefore you can't use
[672](https://docs.rs#672)//!   `VALUE` as a type parameter on a generic struct in combination with generic setters.
[673](https://docs.rs#673)//! - The `try_setter` attribute and `owned` builder pattern are not compatible in practice;
[674](https://docs.rs#674)//!   an error during building will consume the builder, making it impossible to continue
[675](https://docs.rs#675)//!   construction.
[676](https://docs.rs#676)//! - When re-exporting the underlying struct under a different name, the
[677](https://docs.rs#677)//!   auto-generated documentation will not match.
[678](https://docs.rs#678)//! - If derive_builder depends on your crate, and vice versa, then a cyclic
[679](https://docs.rs#679)//!   dependency would occur. To break it you could try to depend on the
[680](https://docs.rs#680)//!   [`derive_builder_core`] crate instead.
[681](https://docs.rs#681)//!
[682](https://docs.rs#682)//! ## Report Issues and Ideas
[683](https://docs.rs#683)//!
[684](https://docs.rs#684)//! [Open an issue on GitHub](https://github.com/colin-kiegel/rust-derive-builder/issues)
[685](https://docs.rs#685)//!
[686](https://docs.rs#686)//! If possible please try to provide the debugging info if you experience unexpected
[687](https://docs.rs#687)//! compilation errors (see above).
[688](https://docs.rs#688)//!
[689](https://docs.rs#689)//! [builder pattern]: https://web.archive.org/web/20170701044756/https://aturon.github.io/ownership/builders.html
[690](https://docs.rs#690)//! [`derive_builder_core`]: https://crates.io/crates/derive_builder_core
[691](https://docs.rs#691)

[694](https://docs.rs#694)

[696](https://docs.rs#696)extern crate alloc;
[697](https://docs.rs#697)

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap

## Expand description

Command Line Argument Parser for Rust

Quick Links:

- Derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)
- Builder [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- [Cookbook](https://docs.rs/_cookbook/index.html)
- [CLI Concepts](https://docs.rs/_concepts/index.html)
- [FAQ](https://docs.rs/_faq/index.html)
- [Discussions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/discussions)
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v4.6.1/CHANGELOG.md)(includes major version migration guides)

[§](https://docs.rs#aspirations)Aspirations

- Out of the box, users get a polished CLI experience
- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output, [shell completions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/master/clap_complete), etc

- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output,
- Flexible enough to port your existing CLI interface
- However, we won’t necessarily streamline support for each use case

- Reasonable parse performance
- Resilient maintainership, including
- Willing to break compatibility rather than batching up breaking changes in large releases
- Leverage feature flags to keep to one active branch
- Being under [WG-CLI](https://github.com/rust-cli/team/)to increase the bus factor

- We follow semver and will wait about 6-9 months between major breaking changes
- We will support the last two minor Rust releases (MSRV, currently 1.74)

While these aspirations can be at odds with fast build times and low binary
size, we will still strive to keep these reasonable for the flexibility you
get.  Check out the
[argparse-benchmarks](https://github.com/rust-cli/argparse-benchmarks-rs) for
CLI parsers optimized for other use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Run

`$ cargo add clap --features derive`*(See also  feature flag reference)*

Then define your CLI in `main.rs`:

```
use clap::Parser;
/// Simple program to greet a person
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)]
struct Args {
    /// Name of the person to greet
    #[arg(short, long)]
    name: String,
    /// Number of times to greet
    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 1)]
    count: u8,
}
fn main() {
    let args = Args::parse();
    for _ in 0..args.count {
        println!("Hello {}!", args.name);
    }
}
```
And try it out:

```
$ demo --help
A simple to use, efficient, and full-featured Command Line Argument Parser
Usage: demo[EXE] [OPTIONS] --name <NAME>
Options:
  -n, --name <NAME>    Name of the person to greet
  -c, --count <COUNT>  Number of times to greet [default: 1]
  -h, --help           Print help
  -V, --version        Print version
$ demo --name Me
Hello Me!
```
*(version number and  .exe extension on windows replaced by placeholders)*

See also the derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html) and [reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)

[§](https://docs.rs#related-projects)Related Projects

Augment clap:

- [wild](https://crates.io/crates/wild)for supporting wildcards (- `*`) on Windows like you do Linux
- [argfile](https://crates.io/crates/argfile)for loading additional arguments from a file (aka response files)
- [shadow-rs](https://crates.io/crates/shadow-rs)for generating- `Command::long_version`
- [clap_mangen](https://crates.io/crates/clap_mangen)for generating man page source (roff)
- [clap_complete](https://crates.io/crates/clap_complete)for shell completion support
- [clap-i18n-richformatter](https://crates.io/crates/clap-i18n-richformatter)for i18n support with- `clap::error::RichFormatter`

CLI Helpers

- [clio](https://crates.io/crates/clio)for reading/writing to files specified as arguments
- [clap-verbosity-flag](https://crates.io/crates/clap-verbosity-flag)
